content: There exist specific wavefunctions that saturate the uncertainty bound. The Robertson-Schrödinger relation states that for any two Hermitian operators ( A ) and ( B ), and a quantum system in the state ( psi ), there are associated probability distributions for the measurement outcomes of ( A ) and ( B ), with standard deviations ( Delta_psi A ) and ( Delta_psi B ). The inequality is expressed as: [ Delta_psi A cdot Delta_psi B geq frac{1}{4} left| langle [A langle A rangle_psi, B langle B rangle_psi] rangle_psi right|^2 ] Here, ([A, B] = AB BA) is the commutator of ( A ) and ( B ), ({A, B} = AB + BA) is the anticommutator, and (langle X rangle_psi) represents the expectation value of ( X ) in the state ( psi ). This inequality is known as the Robertson-Schrödinger relation and generalizes the Heisenberg uncertainty principle as a special case. The version of the inequality involving only the commutator term was first derived in 1930 by Howard Percy Robertson. Later, Erwin Schrödinger extended it by including the anticommutator term. Other Uncertainty Principles The Robertson-Schrödinger relation provides a framework for uncertainty relations between any two non-commuting observables. Examples include: The uncertainty relation between the position and momentum of a particle. The uncertainty relation between the energy and position of a particle in a one-dimensional potential ( V(x) ). The uncertainty relation between angular position and angular momentum for systems with small angular uncertainty. The uncertainty relation between two orthogonal components of the total angular momentum operator. The uncertainty relation between the number of electrons in a superconductor and the phase of its Ginzburg-Landau order parameter. Energy-Time Uncertainty Principle The energy-time uncertainty principle is a well-known relation that is not an obvious consequence of the Robertson-Schrödinger relation. Since energy and time are related in special relativity in a manner analogous to momentum and space, early quantum theorists, including Niels Bohr, recognized the validity of the energy-time uncertainty relation. However, the interpretation of ( Delta t ) was unclear because time is not an operator in quantum mechanics but rather a parameter describing the system's evolution. Lev Landau humorously remarked, To violate the time-energy uncertainty relation, all I have to do is measure the energy very precisely and then look at my watch. Despite this, Einstein and Bohr understood the heuristic significance of the principle. A state that exists only for a short duration cannot have a well-defined energy. To achieve a precise energy, the frequency of the state must be well-defined, which requires the state to persist for many cycles, inversely proportional to the required precision. For example, in spectroscopy, excited states have finite lifetimes. According to the time-energy uncertainty principle, these states do not have a precise energy, and the energy of the emitted photon during decay varies slightly. The average energy of the emitted photon peaks at the theoretical energy of the state, but the distribution has a finite width, known as the natural linewidth. States that decay quickly have broad linewidths, while those that decay slowly have narrow linewidths. The broad linewidth of fast-decaying states makes it challenging to measure their energy accurately. Researchers have even used microwave cavities to slow the decay rate and achieve sharper spectral peaks. This linewidth effect also complicates the measurement of the rest mass of fast-decaying particles in particle physics. The faster a particle decays, the less certain its mass becomes. A common but incorrect formulation of the energy-time uncertainty principle suggests that measuring the energy of a quantum system to an accuracy ( Delta E ) requires a time interval ( Delta t > hbar / Delta E ). This interpretation, similar to Landau's joke, was explicitly invalidated by Y. Aharonov and D. Bohm in 1961. The time ( Delta t ) in the uncertainty relation refers to the duration during which the system remains undisturbed, not the time during which experimental equipment is active. In 1936, Paul Dirac provided a precise definition and derivation of the energy-time uncertainty relation within a relativistic quantum theory of events. In this framework, particles follow trajectories in spacetime, with each trajectory parameterized independently by a proper time. This many-times formulation of quantum mechanics is mathematically equivalent to standard formulations but is more suited for relativistic generalizations. It inspired Shin-Ichiro Tomonaga's covariant perturbation theory for quantum electrodynamics. A more widely used formulation of the energy-time uncertainty principle was introduced in 1945 by L. I. Mandelshtam and I. E. Tamm. For a quantum system in a non-stationary state ( |psirangle ) and an observable ( B ) represented by a self-adjoint operator ( hat{B} ), the following relation holds: [ Delta_psi E cdot Delta_psi B geq frac{hbar}{2} left| frac{dlangle hat{B} rangle}{dt} right| ] Here, ( Delta_psi E ) is the standard deviation of the energy operator in the state ( |psirangle ), ( Delta_psi B ) is the standard deviation of the operator ( hat{B} ), and ( langle hat{B} rangle ) is the expectation value of ( hat{B} ) in that state. Although the second factor on the left-hand side has the dimension of time, it differs from the time parameter in the Schrödinger equation. Instead, it represents the lifetime of the state ( |psirangle ) with respect to the observable ( B ), i.e., the time after which the expectation value ( langle hat{B} rangle ) changes significantly. Popular Culture The uncertainty principle frequently appears in popular culture, often imprecisely or conflated with the observer effect. Examples include: In Star Trek: The Next Generation, fictional Heisenberg compensators are used to overcome the uncertainty principle in the operation of transporters. When asked how they work, technical advisor Michael Okuda humorously replied, They work just fine, thank you. In the Futurama episode The Luck of the Fryrish, the Professor loses a horse race due to a quantum finish and complains, No fair. You changed the outcome by measuring it. This conflates the uncertainty principle with the observer effect. A well-known joke involves Heisenberg being pulled over by a policeman. When asked if he knows how fast he was driving, Heisenberg replies, No, but I know exactly where I am. In the 1997 film The Lost World: Jurassic Park, chaos theorist Ian Malcolm claims that observing and documenting dinosaurs without interacting with them is scientifically impossible due to the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle, conflating it with the observer effect.
